project: DWRO S7 — Factory and Factory Session Placement Grammar
description: Implement DWRO story S7 so you run and Factory Session lifecycle commands use one explicit local-or-remote placement grammar, remote run creates a distinct server-owned Factory Session on exactly the selected You server, and equivalent local and remote operations preserve lifecycle, output, and exit classifications.

context.customerAsk: Implement DWRO story S7: you run and Factory Session invocation and lifecycle-control commands accept root --remote; a remote run creates a server-owned Factory Session and preserves the lifecycle, output, and exit classifications customers receive from an equivalent local run.
context.problem: Factory CLI operations do not yet present one consistent local-versus-remote placement model. Remote run targets the default live-session compatibility invocation rather than starting a distinct server-owned Factory Session, while Factory Session controls behave as implicitly HTTP-only commands. This leaves ownership ambiguous and risks different output and exit classifications for equivalent local and remote outcomes.
context.solution: Resolve placement once at the CLI boundary, normalize Factory invocation and lifecycle-control requests independently of placement, and dispatch each request through exactly one injected adapter. Local placement calls the Factory Sessions service root; remote placement calls the canonical Factory Session HTTP contract at exactly the selected --server URI with no fallback. Remote run starts a server-owned Factory Session and maps canonical session lifecycle and result facts into the same stdout, stderr, structured output, and exit classifications used locally.

acceptanceCriteria: Authored CLI contracts, executable parsing, help, and reference guidance identify you run and the supported Factory Session pause, resume, cancel, and terminate commands as placement-aware; local is the default and root --remote --server <uri> selects a running server without implying async, follow, listener, or hosting behavior.

One you --remote --server <uri> run request is sent to exactly <uri>, creates one distinct server-owned Factory Session through the canonical durable execution contract, returns its identity, and leaves that session inspectable on the server even if the submitting CLI disconnects while execution continues.

Equivalent local and remote runs normalize the same target, invocation arguments, requested policy, and output selection and produce contract-equivalent lifecycle, primary-result or stream output, structured output, diagnostics, and success/failure/timeout/cancel/interrupt exit classifications, allowing only placement and generated identity metadata to differ.

Local and remote Factory Session pause, resume, cancel, and terminate operations target the exact supplied Factory Session identity, return the same accepted, idempotent, invalid-state, not-found, and terminal outcome classifications, and preserve canonical lifecycle events and state.

Unsupported placement, invalid or unavailable endpoints, remote transport interruption, malformed server responses, and command conflicts fail with stable actionable diagnostics before unintended Factory or lifecycle side effects; remote failures never fall back to local execution or another endpoint.

Typecheck and tests pass with direct package, CLI contract, HTTP contract, and focused functional evidence; no NEW lint violations relative to current main, and the gates green on main (backend-size, pkg-maint, pkg-file-count, pkg-structure, vet) stay green.

The implementation/review loop continues until required CI is terminal and passing, all blocking PR conversation feedback is explicitly addressed, merge conflicts and shared or generated-file churn are resolved against current main, and the PR is actually merged.

userStories.title: Expose consistent Factory placement semantics
userStories.description: As a CLI customer, I want Factory invocation and Factory Session lifecycle commands to use the same root placement grammar so I can predict where an operation executes before it begins.
acceptanceCriteria: you run and you session pause|resume|cancel|terminate accept the persistent root --remote flag before or after the command path wherever persistent flags are supported.
Without --remote, each supported command selects its injected local Factory Sessions operation; with --remote, it selects only the HTTP adapter for the exact global --server <uri> value.

The authored command contract marks these commands as dual-placement and executable validation rejects unsupported placement or contradictory local-hosting modes before Factory execution, listener startup, browser launch, recording, or lifecycle mutation.
Help and packaged reference guidance explain local default placement, explicit remote placement, exact server selection, and the distinction between placement and waiting, following, or hosting.
Existing S1 rules remain intact: remote run conflicts with --with-server and --with-site, --listen remains the local bind selector, and remote failures never fall back locally.
Focused parser, command-contract, help, and dispatch tests prove both persistent-flag positions and exactly-one-adapter selection through observable requests and side effects.
Typecheck passes
Tests pass
userStories.notes: Implemented the dual-placement CLI contract and generated family/published metadata for run plus pause, resume, cancel, and terminate. The session registry now selects an injected local Factory Sessions adapter by default and the exact HTTP adapter/server when --remote is resolved. Added both flag-position and exactly-one-adapter dispatch coverage, refreshed command/input/help baselines, and validated CLI, wire, contract, functional-scenario, and docs checks.

userStories.title: Create a server-owned Factory Session for remote run
userStories.description: As an operator, I want a remote run to create its own Factory Session on the selected server so execution ownership and later inspection do not depend on the submitting CLI process.
acceptanceCriteria: you --remote --server <uri> run maps the normalized run target, arguments, invocation policy, request identity, and wait behavior into the canonical durable Factory Session execution request and sends it to exactly <uri>.

The server admits exactly one new Factory Session, returns its canonical session identity, and owns execution lifetime independently of the HTTP request and submitting CLI lifetime; disconnecting the CLI does not cancel admitted work unless the customer explicitly requested cancellation behavior.
The remote path does not invoke ~default through the live-session compatibility invocation route and does not open a local runtime, listener, browser, or recording owner.

The accepted Factory Session is discoverable and inspectable by its returned identity through the existing session read, event, dispatch, artifact, and result surfaces while running and after terminal completion.

Stable request identity follows the canonical server idempotency contract: an equivalent retry does not create duplicate execution, while conflicting reuse returns the established conflict classification.

Invalid target, invalid invocation input, admission failure, unavailable server, request timeout, and connection loss return actionable remote diagnostics without local fallback or duplicate session creation.

Focused HTTP contract and CLI functional tests enter through root.BuildProcess and Process.Execute, synchronize on observable lifecycle facts rather than sleeps, and prove server ownership, disconnect survival, exact endpoint selection, and no fallback.
Typecheck passes
Tests pass

userStories.title: Preserve local and remote run result classifications
userStories.description: As an automation author, I want equivalent local and remote runs to report the same meaningful result so changing placement does not break output parsing or exit handling.
acceptanceCriteria: The same supported Factory target and customer input normalize to contract-equivalent invocation values locally and remotely, including structured arguments, defaults, repeated values, stdin binding, requested policy, and output mode.

Completed local and remote runs expose the same primary result content and terminal success classification; human, JSON, primary-result, and response-stream or NDJSON modes retain their documented stdout/stderr separation and terminal-record behavior.

Failed, blocked, needs-human, paused, interrupted, timed-out, canceled, unresolved-primary-result, and runtime-failure outcomes map from canonical Factory Session facts to the same public error code/message category and process exit kind in both placements.

Remote transport and malformed-response failures remain distinguishable from domain execution failures, identify the selected endpoint safely, do not leak credentials or customer payloads, and never synthesize a successful terminal result.
Session identity, request identity, and recovery context are retained in structured output and actionable diagnostics wherever the canonical contract supplies them.

Focused parity tests compare observable local and remote CLI output and exit behavior for success plus representative domain, timeout/cancel, and transport failures; canonical event ordering proves terminal output is not emitted before the authoritative terminal session fact.
Typecheck passes
Tests pass

userStories.title: Control the exact Factory Session in either placement
userStories.description: As an operator, I want to pause, resume, cancel, or terminate a known Factory Session locally or remotely so lifecycle control remains predictable across deployment layouts.
acceptanceCriteria: Local you session pause|resume|cancel|terminate <session-id> calls the injected Factory Sessions lifecycle operation, while the same command with root --remote --server <uri> calls exactly that server's canonical control route.
Both placements target the exact supplied canonical Factory Session identity; they do not substitute ~default, a current session, a similarly named session, or a session from another endpoint.
Accepted controls preserve canonical lifecycle event ordering and return equivalent human and JSON output for pause, resume, cancel, and terminate.

Repeated terminal controls are idempotent according to the Factory Sessions contract, and already-applied, invalid-state, not-found, unavailable, and control-versus-completion race outcomes have equivalent classifications locally and remotely.
A failed remote control never retries through the local service, and validation or transport failure causes no lifecycle mutation on either placement.

Focused service, CLI, HTTP, functional, race, and repeat-run tests prove exact-session routing, idempotency, control-versus-completion behavior, event/state consistency, and zero cross-session mutation without arbitrary sleeps.
Typecheck passes
Tests pass
